title: The worker who judged kindly
hookLine: judge others on the side of merit
carry: dan l'kaf zechut: tip the scale toward merit

lines: NO MONEY, NO LAND, NO CATTLE.
cards: A worker has labored for a landowner for years. On the eve of Yom Kippur he says: pay me, so I can go home and feed my wife and children. I have no money, says the landowner.
Then give me produce. I have none. Land?
Bedding? None. The worker swings his bag over his shoulder and walks home with nothing, sad.

teach.b: Dan l'kaf zechut. Judging on the side of merit. You met its first form long ago, as lechaf zechut.
Turn it four ways. First, the end of the story. After the festival, the landowner arrives with the wages and donkeys loaded with food, drink and good things.

teach.h: KAF: THE PAN OF A SCALE.
teach.b: They eat together. Then he asks: when I said I had nothing, what did you suspect? The worker has an answer for every refusal.
No money? I thought you'd found a bargain and spent it. No cattle?
Hired out to others. No land? Leased.
Each time, an innocent explanation. For the bedding, he guessed the landowner had vowed all his property to Heaven, and that was exactly what had happened; the sages had since released the vow.

Then the line: as you judged me on the side of merit, may God judge you on the side of merit. Second, the phrase. In Pirkei Avot, Joshua ben Perachiah teaches: judge every person on the side of merit.
Kaf is the pan of a balance. When the evidence could tip either way, you put your hand on the good side. Third, the Torah.
Leviticus says, "in righteousness shalt thou judge thy neighbour," and the Talmud reads it as this same instruction: lean toward merit.

teach.h: JUDGE ON THE SIDE OF MERIT.
teach.b: Commentators on Avot say this applies most to someone you don't know well, or someone whose record is good. It isn't a demand to ignore a pattern.
It's a refusal to write the worst story first, when you were only handed half of one.

how: Jews study Joshua ben Perachiah's teaching in Pirkei Avot to judge every person on the side of merit, and the Talmud's story of the worker and the landowner is often retold to illustrate it.

o: judging others on the side of merit
judging only by the facts you can prove
excusing every wrong, whatever it is

games.q: dan l'kaf zechut — tap the pairs.
p: found an innocent reason each time
had vowed his property to Heaven

s: the worker suspected the landowner of cheating him
for every refusal he chose an innocent explanation.
one of the worker's innocent guesses turned out to be exactly true
he guessed the landowner had vowed all his property to Heaven, and he had; the vow was later released.
judging toward merit means ignoring every pattern
commentators apply it most to strangers or people with a good record: not worst-first, not blind.

games.q: you're the worker. after years of labor, your employer says he has no money, no land, no cattle. you walk home with nothing. what do you think?
o: there must be an innocent reason.
games.why: he judged on the side of merit at every step, and the landowner blessed him: as you judged me favorably, may God judge you favorably.

practice: Think of someone who bothered you lately, an unanswered message, a short tone, a friend who didn't show, and notice the story you've already told yourself.
Be the worker on the long walk home and find one innocent explanation, then another: they were drowning at work, they didn't see it, something happened at home.
You don't have to know which is true; let the scale move, and if you pray, ask to judge the way you hope to be judged.

wordCard.voice: Dan l'kaf zechut. Judging on the side of merit: when it could go either way, tipping the scale toward the good. From Pirkei Avot. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: judging toward the pan of merit, from Avot 1:6.

carryVoice: Your line: dan l'kaf zechut: tip the scale toward merit. Half a story doesn't need the worst ending. Day well spent.

sources.q: in righteousness shalt thou judge thy neighbour
